title: Public participation divides into mobilization, connection, spectatorship, and outsider patterns
source_unit: Pew Research Center Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey and American Trends Panel; U.S. adults, 2025 fieldwork

observations.period: Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey July 9-December 5, 2025; report published July 2026

denominator.unit: adults in the nationally representative Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey; cluster categories exclude respondents not classified

engagement_groups.unit: percent of U.S. adults classified into four clusters based on 19 participation measures

voting_2024.unit: percent within engagement group reporting voting in 2024

contacting_official.unit: percent within engagement group contacting an elected official in the past year

news_attention.value: Mobilizers 95%; Connectors 88%; Spectators 84%; Outsiders 41% follow national news at least somewhat closely

partisan_mix.value: Each group contains Republicans, Democrats, and people without a lean; Mobilizers are 41% Republican/lean Republican and 57% Democratic/lean Democratic

observations.method: Pew cluster analysis of 19 political, civic, religious, and news-participation measures, with a second American Trends Panel sample used to compare groups on civic knowledge and attitudes.
observations.uncertainty: The clusters describe a specific period that included the 2024 presidential election; they are not a time series or causal typology. Participation, news attention, religion, and political action are correlated inside the clusters but not necessarily causally ordered.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults classified as Mobilizers, Connectors, Spectators, or Outsiders; age, party, education, race, and community differences are reported separately by Pew.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low measured participation does not equal apathy: Outsiders include people who voted or attend religious services, while Spectators follow news without public posting. High activity also does not establish policy influence or institutional trust.

boundary: This record adds a multidimensional civic-culture map. It does not measure change over time, explain why people enter a group, establish civic influence, or infer trust and political meaning from participation alone.
